The '''FIBA Basketball World Cup''' is an international [[basketball]] competition between the senior [[List of men's national basketball teams|men's national teams]] of the members of the [[FIBA|International Basketball Federation]] (FIBA), the sport's global governing body. It takes place every four years and is considered the flagship event of FIBA.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.usabasketball.com/about/inside.html |title=Inside USA Basketball |work=basketball.com |publisher=[[USA Basketball]] |access-date=7 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100907043355/http://www.usabasketball.com/about/inside.html |archive-date=7 September 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

From its inception in 1950 until 2010, the tournament was known as the '''FIBA World Championship'''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=World Cup History |url=https://www.fiba.basketball/basketballworldcup/2023/world-cup-history |access-date=2023-08-09 |website=FIBA.basketball |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=26 January 2012 |title=PR N°1&nbsp;– FIBA Basketball World Cup officially launched in Madrid |url=http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/news/lateNews/p/newsid/50470/arti.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304051629/http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/news/lateNews/p/newsid/50470/arti.html |archive-date=4 March 2016 |access-date=26 January 2012 |publisher=FIBA}}</ref>

The tournament structure is similar, but not identical, to that of the [[FIFA World Cup]]; the current format of the tournament involves 32 teams competing for the title at venues within the host nation.  The FIBA Basketball World Cup and the FIFA World Cup were played in the same year as each other from 1970 through 2014. A parallel event for women's teams, now known as the [[FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup]], is also held quadrennially. From 1986 through 2014, the men's and women's edition were held in the same year, though in different countries. Following the 2014 FIBA World Cup for men and championships for women, the men's World Cup was scheduled on a new four-year cycle to avoid conflict with the FIFA World Cup. The men's World Cup was held in 2019, in the year following the FIFA World Cup. The women's championship, which was renamed from "FIBA World Championship for Women" to "FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup" after its 2014 edition, will remain on the previous four-year cycle, with championships in the same year as the FIFA World Cup.
 
The winning team receives the [[Naismith Trophy]], first awarded in [[1967 FIBA World Championship|1967]]. The current champion is [[Germany men's national basketball team|Germany]], which defeated [[Serbia men's national basketball team|Serbia]] in the final of the [[2023 FIBA Basketball World Cup|2023 tournament]].

==History==
{{main|History of the FIBA Basketball World Cup}}
{{more citations needed section|date=April 2017}}
[[File:FIBA World Cup host countries.png|thumb|300px|World map depicting the number of times a country has hosted the World Cup. Dark blue: twice; light blue: once.]]
The FIBA Basketball World Cup was conceived at a meeting of the FIBA World Congress at the [[1948 Summer Olympics]] in London.<ref name="FIBA History">{{cite web|url=http://www.fiba.com/downloads/v3_abouFiba/mp/FIBA_world_championships_history.pdf|title=FIBA World Championship History (pdf)|publisher=[[FIBA]]|date=1 January 2007 |access-date=7 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927204202/http://www.fiba.com/downloads/v3_abouFiba/mp/FIBA_world_championships_history.pdf |archive-date=27 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Long-time FIBA Secretary-General [[Renato William Jones]] urged FIBA to adopt a World Championship, similar to the [[FIFA World Cup]], to be held in every four years between [[Olympiad]]s.  The FIBA Congress, seeing how successful the 23-team [[Basketball at the 1948 Summer Olympics|Olympic tournament]] was that year, agreed to the proposal, beginning with a tournament in [[1950 FIBA World Championship|1950]]. [[Argentina]] was selected as host, largely because it was the only country willing to take on the task.<ref name="Kennedy">{{cite news |first=John |last=Kennedy |title='El Primer Crack' of Argentine Basketball: Oscar Furlong |date=12 March 2008 |work=Society for Irish Latin American Studies |url=http://www.irlandeses.org/0803kennedyc2.htm |publisher=John Kennedy |access-date=7 September 2010 |archive-date=25 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225124356/http://www.irlandeses.org/0803kennedyc2.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Argentina took advantage of the host selection, winning all their games en route to becoming the first FIBA World Champion.

The first five tournaments were held in [[South America]], and teams from the [[FIBA Americas|Americas]] dominated the tournament, winning eight of nine medals at the first three tournaments.  By [[1963 FIBA World Championship|1963]], however, teams from [[Eastern Europe]] and [[Southeast Europe]] &mdash; the [[Soviet Union national basketball team|Soviet Union]] and [[Yugoslavia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]], in particular &mdash; began to catch up to the teams from the American continents.  Between 1963 and 1990, the tournament was dominated by the [[United States men's national basketball team|United States]], the [[Soviet Union national basketball team|Soviet Union]], [[Yugoslavia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]], and [[Brazil national basketball team|Brazil]], which together accounted for every medal at the tournament.

The [[1994 FIBA World Championship]] held in [[Toronto]] marked the beginning of a new era, as currently active American [[NBA]] players participated in the tournament for the first time (prior to that only European and South American professionals were allowed to participate as they were still classified as amateurs),<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.usab.com/history/why-can-pros-complete-in-international-events.aspx |title=Why Can Pros Complete in International Tournaments |last=Hubbard |first=Jan |publisher=USA Basketball |access-date=23 July 2021 |archive-date=1 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210801120416/https://www.usab.com/history/why-can-pros-complete-in-international-events.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |first=Jack |last=McCallum |title=Lords of the Rings |date=18 February 1991 |magazine=Sports Illustrated |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1118882/1/index.htm |access-date=7 September 2010 |archive-date=14 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120214002540/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1118882/1/index.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> while the [[Soviet Union]] and [[Yugoslavia]] split into many new states. The United States dominated that year and won gold, while former states of the USSR and Yugoslavia, [[Russia national basketball team|Russia]] and [[Croatia national basketball team|Croatia]], won silver and bronze. The [[1998 FIBA World Championship]], held in [[Greece]] ([[Athens]] and [[Piraeus]]), lost some of its luster when the [[1998–99 NBA lockout]] prevented [[NBA]] players from participating. The new [[Serbia national basketball team|Yugoslavian]] team, now consisting of the former Yugoslav republics of [[Serbia]] and [[Montenegro]], won the gold medal over Russia, while the USA, with professional basketball players playing in Europe and two college players, finished third.

In [[2002 FIBA World Championship|2002]], other nations caught up to the four powerhouse countries and their successor states. [[FR Yugoslavia national basketball team|FR Yugoslavia]], led by [[Peja Stojaković]] of the [[Sacramento Kings]] and [[Dejan Bodiroga]] of [[FC Barcelona Bàsquet|FC Barcelona]], won the final game against [[Argentina national basketball team|Argentina]], while [[Dirk Nowitzki]], who was the [[FIBA World Cup MVP|tournament's MVP]], led [[Germany national basketball team|Germany]] to the bronze, its first ever World Championship medal.  Meanwhile, the United States team, this time made up of NBA players, struggled to a sixth-place finish. This new era of parity convinced FIBA to expand the tournament to 24 teams for the 2006, [[2010 FIBA World Championship|2010]], and [[2014 FIBA Basketball World Cup|2014]] editions of the tournament.<ref name="Secretary">{{cite news |first=FIBA |last=Secretary |title=Press Release no. 42: "BAD Badtz-Maru" launched as official mascot for Japan 2006 |date=13 December 2005 |publisher=FIBA |url=http://www.fiba.com/ce/pages/en/events/blockbusters/world_champ_men_06/article_World_Champ_Men.asp?cookietest=done&r_act_news=10383&r_cat=8 |access-date=7 September 2010 |location=Geneva/Tokyo |archive-date=30 August 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090830205635/http://www.fiba.com/ce/pages/en/events/blockbusters/world_champ_men_06/article_World_Champ_Men.asp?cookietest=done&r_act_news=10383&r_cat=8 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=FIBA |last=Secretary |title=ESP&nbsp;– Spain selected to host 2014 World Championship |date=5 May 2009 |publisher=[[FIBA]] |url=http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/news/lateNews/p/newsid/30278/arti.html |access-date=7 September 2010 |location=Geneva |archive-date=27 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090527082509/http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/news/lateNews/p/newsid/30278/arti.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In [[2006 FIBA World Championship|2006]], emerging powerhouse [[Spain national basketball team|Spain]] beat [[Greece national basketball team|Greece]] in the first appearance in the final for both teams. Spain became only the seventh team ([[Yugoslavia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]] and [[Serbia and Montenegro national basketball team|FR Yugoslavia]] are counted separately in the FIBA records)<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp//tid/390/_//teams.html |title=FIBA.com Archive – Yugoslavia. |access-date=22 August 2012 |archive-date=16 September 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140916043510/http://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp/tid/390/_/teams.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> to capture a World Championship gold. The USA, which lost to Greece in a semi-final, won against Argentina in the third-place match and claimed bronze.

In the [[2010 FIBA World Championship]] final, the USA defeated [[Turkey national basketball team|Turkey]] and won gold for the first time in 16 years, while [[Lithuania men's national basketball team|Lithuania]] beat Serbia and won bronze. The next time around, the United States became the third country to defend the championship, winning against Serbia at the [[2014 FIBA World Cup|2014 edition]] of the tournament. [[French national basketball team|France]] beat Lithuania in the bronze medal game.

After the 2014 edition, FIBA instituted significant changes to the World Cup. The final competition was expanded from 24 to 32 teams. Also, for the first time since 1967, the competition would no longer overlap with the FIFA World Cup. To accommodate this change, the 2014 FIBA World Cup was followed by a [[2019 FIBA Basketball World Cup|2019 edition]] in China.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/news/presRele/p/newsid/51257/presReleArti.html |title=Mainini: calendar, system of competition and 3x3 our biggest priorities |publisher=[[FIBA]] |date=20 April 2012 |access-date=28 July 2012 |archive-date=3 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120803050753/http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/news/presRele/p/newsid/51257/presReleArti.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Qualification==
{{main|FIBA Basketball World Cup qualification}}
[[File:FIBA World Cup participation.png|thumb|300px|World map depicting the number of times a national team has participated in the World Cup as of 2014.]]
The Basketball World Cup has used various forms of qualification throughfive tournaments were held in South America and participation was dominated by teams from the Americas. At the first tournament, FIBA intended for the three Olympic medalists to compete, plus the host Argentina and two teams each from Europe, Asia, and South America. However, no Asian team was willing to travel to the event, so six of the ten teams were from the Americas (all three Olympic medalists were from the Americas, plus the zone received two continental berths and an Asia's berth). The former European powerhouse [[Soviet Union national basketball team|Soviet Union]], later made their first tournament appearance in [[1959 FIBA World Championship|1959]], after missing the first two events.

In the tournament's early years, only [[EuroBasket|Europe]] and [[South American Basketball Championship|South America]] had established continental tournaments, so participation in the tournament was largely by invitation.  Later, [[FIBA Asia Championship|Asia]] added a continental championship in 1960, followed by [[FIBA Africa Championship|Africa]] in 1962, [[Centrobasket|Central America]] in 1965, and [[FIBA Oceania Championship|Oceania]] in 1971, As a result of these changes, qualification became more formalized starting with the [[1967 FIBA World Championship|1967 tournament]].  In that year, the Asian champion received an automatic berth in the tournament, joining the top European and South American teams.  In [[1970 FIBA World Championship|1970]], the African and Oceanian champion each received a berth, while the Centrobasket champion and runner-up were each invited.  For most of these years, the tournament host, defending World Champion, and top [[Basketball at the Summer Olympics|Olympic basketball tournament]] finishers also qualified for the event.

From 1970 through the 2014 World Cup, qualification continued to be based on the continental competitions and the Olympic tournament.  The only major change came in the [[1990 FIBA World Championship]], when the tournament started taking qualifiers from the newly redesigned [[FIBA Americas Championship]] rather than from North, Central, and South America individually.  After the tournament expanded to 24 teams in [[2006 FIBA World Championship|2006]], the tournament allocated qualification as follows:<ref>{{cite web |url=http://turkey2010.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/Qualifiers/p/qualifiers.html |title=How they got there |publisher=FIBA.com |access-date=8 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100910175341/http://turkey2010.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/Qualifiers/p/qualifiers.html |archive-date=10 September 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

* '''[[EuroBasket|FIBA EuroBasket]] (Europe)'''&nbsp;– 6 berths
* '''[[AfroBasket|FIBA AfroBasket]] (Africa)'''&nbsp;– 3 berths
* '''[[FIBA Asia Cup]] (Asia) '''&nbsp;– 3 berths
* '''[[FIBA AmeriCup]] (Americas)'''&nbsp;– 5 berths
* '''[[FIBA Oceania Championship]] (Oceania)'''&nbsp;– 2 berths
* '''[[Basketball at the Summer Olympics|Defending Olympic Champion]]'''&nbsp;– 1 berth, removed from the zone of the Olympic champion
* '''Host team'''&nbsp;– 1 berth
* '''FIBA-selected [[Wild card (sports)|wild cards]]'''&nbsp;– 4 berths

Each of the five continental championships also served as qualification for the Olympics, so all were held every two years. The year immediately preceding the World Championship was used to determine the berths at the tournament. For example, all of the berths at the [[2010 FIBA World Championship]] were determined by continental championships held in [[2010 FIBA World Championship qualification|2009]].  After the first 20 teams qualified, FIBA then selected four wild card teams, based on sporting, economic, and governance criteria, as well as a required registration fee from each team to be considered by the FIBA board.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://turkey2010.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/event-guide/p/wild-card.html |title=Wild cards for Turkey 2010 |publisher=FIBA.com |access-date=8 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100830145914/http://turkey2010.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/event-guide/p/wild-card.html |archive-date=30 August 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Of the four wild cards, only three could come from one continental zone.  In each of the two tournaments that the wild card system was in place, FIBA selected the maximum three European teams to compete in the event.

FIBA instituted major changes to its competition calendar and the qualifying process for both the World Cup and Olympics in 2017.

First, the continental championships are now held once every four years, specifically in years that immediately follow the Summer Olympics. The continental championships no longer play a role in qualifying for either the World Cup or Olympics.<ref name="New calendar">{{cite press release |url=http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/news/presRele/p/newsid/54422/presReleArti.html |title=Central Board gives green light to new format and calendar of competition |publisher=FIBA |date=11 November 2012 |access-date=31 August 2013 |archive-date=23 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923060241/http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/news/presRele/p/newsid/54422/presReleArti.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The [[2019 FIBA Basketball World Cup|2019 World Cup]] qualifying process, which began in 2017, is the first under a new format. Qualifying takes place over a two-year cycle, involving six windows of play. Qualifying zones mirror the FIBA continental zones, except that FIBA Asia and FIBA Oceania are now combined into a single Asia-Pacific qualifying zone. In each qualifying zone, nations are divided into Division A and Division B, with [[promotion and relegation]] between the two. FIBA did not initially reveal full details of the new process, but announced that at least in opening phases, it would feature groups of three or four teams, playing home-and-away within the group.<ref name="New calendar"/> Below is the list of distribution of berths according to each FIBA qualifying zone.

* '''[[FIBA Europe]]''' – 12 berths
* '''[[FIBA Americas]]''' – 7 berths
* '''[[FIBA Africa]]''' – 5 berths
* '''Asia-Pacific ([[FIBA Asia]] and [[FIBA Oceania]])''' – 7 berths
* '''Host team''' – 1 berth

==Tournament format==
[[File:FIBA World Cup 2023 Trophy Tour - Jakarta - Naismith Trophy.jpg|thumb|[[Naismith Trophy]]]]
{{For|the various formats used in previous tournaments|History of the FIBA Basketball World Cup#Format of each final tournament}}
The Basketball World Cup has existed in several different formats throughout the years, as it has expanded and contracted between 10 and 24 teams.  The first tournament, in [[1950 FIBA World Championship|1950]], began with a ten-team [[double-elimination tournament]], followed by a six-team [[Round-robin tournament|round robin]] round to determine the champion.  Between 1954 and 1974, each tournament started with a group stage preliminary round; the top teams in each preliminary round group then moved on to a final round robin group to determine the champion.  In [[1978 FIBA World Championship|1978]], FIBA added a gold medal game between the top two finishers in the final group and a bronze medal game between the third and fourth place teams.  In each year between 1959 and 1982, the host team received a bye into the final group.  Of the seven host teams in this era, only three won medals, despite the head start.  As a result, FIBA made the host team compete in the preliminary round starting in [[1986 FIBA World Championship|1986]].

In 1986, the tournament briefly expanded to 24 teams.  Four groups of six teams each competed in the preliminary round group stage.  The top three teams in each group then competed in the second group stage, followed by a four-team knockout tournament between the top two finishers in each group.  The championship contracted back down to 16 teams for the [[1990 FIBA World Championship|1990 tournament]].  The three tournaments between 1990 and 1998 each had two group stages followed by a four-team knockout tournament to determine the medalists.  The [[2002 FIBA World Championship|2002 tournament]] expanded the knockout round to eight teams.

In [[2006 FIBA World Championship|2006]], FIBA made the decision to expand back to 24 teams and introduced the format that was in place through [[2014 FIBA Basketball World Cup|2014]].<ref name="Secretary"/> Under that format, the teams were divided into four preliminary round groups of six teams each.  The top 4 teams in each group then advanced to the Round of 16 in a single-elimination knockout round.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://turkey2010.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/p/system-competition.html |title=System of Competition |work=FIBA.com |publisher=[[FIBA]] |access-date=7 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140711190225/http://turkey2010.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/p/system-competition.html |archive-date=11 July 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In [[2019 FIBA Basketball World Cup|2019]], the final tournament expanded to 32 teams.<ref name="New calendar"/><br/>
If the teams should be tied at the end of the preliminary round, the ties are broken by the following criteria in order:
#Game results between tied teams
#[[Goal average]] between games of the tied teams
#Goal average for all games of the tied teams
#Drawing of lots
The top two teams in each group then advance to a second group-stage round, formed by the top 2 teams from pairs of first-round groups; the match between teams coming from each first-round group carries over as a result in that group, and each plays the 2 teams from the other group. The top 2 teams in each of 4 second-round groups then advance to the quarterfinals in the final, single-elimination round. In that final round, the semifinal losers play in the bronze medal game, while the quarterfinal losers play in a consolation bracket to determine fifth through eighth places.

==Naismith Trophy==
{{main|Naismith Trophy}}
[[File:FIBA Basketball Championships countries.PNG|thumb|300px|Map of best finishes per team. Defunct countries are denoted by circles.]]
Since [[1967 FIBA World Championship|1967]], the champion of each tournament has been awarded the [[Naismith Trophy]], named in honor of basketball's inventor, [[James Naismith]].  A trophy had been planned since the [[1950 FIBA World Championship|first World Championship in 1950]], but did not come to fruition until FIBA finally commissioned a trophy in 1965, after receiving a US$1,000 donation.  The original trophy was used from 1967 through [[1994 FIBA World Championship|1994]] and now sits at the [[Pedro Ferrándiz]] Foundation in Spain. An updated trophy was introduced for the [[1998 FIBA World Championship]]<ref name="egypt">{{cite web |url= http://egyptology.blogspot.com/2006/01/ancient-egypt-in-basketball.html |title= Ancient Egypt in basketball |publisher= egyptology.blogspot.com |date= 17 January 2006 |access-date= 8 September 2010 |archive-date= 24 February 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210224141511/http://egyptology.blogspot.com/2006/01/ancient-egypt-in-basketball.html |url-status= live }}</ref> and the newest version of the trophy was made in 2017 by British silversmith, [[Thomas Lyte]], for the 2019 tournament in China<ref>{{Cite web |title=Makers of the FIBA World Cup Trophy |url=https://thomaslyte.com/makers-of-the-fiba-world-cup-trophy/ |access-date=2025-07-31 |website=Thomas Lyte |language=en}}</ref>

The second trophy is designed in an Egyptian-inspired lotus shape, upon which there are carved maps of the continents and precious stones symbolizing the five continents ([[FIBA Americas]] represents both North America and South America).  Dr. Naismith's name is engraved on all four sides in [[Latin alphabet|Latin]], [[Arabic language|Arabic]], [[Chinese language|Chinese]], and [[Egyptian hieroglyphs]].  The trophy stands 47 centimeters (18.5&nbsp;inches) tall and weighs nine kilograms (twenty pounds).<ref name="trophy">{{cite web |url=http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/event-guide/p/trophy.html |title=Naismith Trophy Unites Five Continents |publisher=FIBA.com |access-date=7 September 2010 |archive-date=26 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100826065727/http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/event-guide/p/trophy.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The most recent Naismith Trophy design was revealed in the [[2019 FIBA World Cup]] Qualifiers Draw Ceremonies, last 7 May 2017. The trophy, which stands about 60 centimeters high (13&nbsp;cm. higher than the 1998 version), is made almost entirely out of gold, and features the names of the previous world cup champions at the base. FIBA's original name (Federation Internationale de Basketball Amateur) is also engraved at the trophy's "hoop". The trophy was designed by Radiant Studios Ltd, and handcrafted by the silversmith [[Thomas Lyte]].

===Medal table===
In the most current medal table released by FIBA as seen on the FIBA official website, the 2014 championship is taken into account, and the records of SFR Yugoslavia and FR Yugoslavia are combined under "Yugoslavia".<ref name="FIBA official website">{{Cite web|title=Medal Count|url=https://www.fiba.basketball/en/history/201-fiba-basketball-world-cup/medalcount|access-date=2025-07-23|website=www.fiba.basketball|language=English}}</ref>

Previously, FIBA had a medal table from 1950 to 2006,<ref name="FIBA World Cup website">{{cite web |url=http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/14/wcm/event-guide/p/flash-back.html#fifteen |title=WORLD CUP HISTORY |access-date=15 October 2013 |archive-date=13 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131013195822/http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/14/wcm/event-guide/p/flash-back.html#fifteen |url-status=dead }}</ref> and another medal table that included results from 1950 to 2006,<ref name="FIBA website history">{{cite web |url=http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/FIBA/fibaHist/p/openNodeIDs/987/selNodeID/987/fibaHist.html |title=FIBA History |access-date=15 October 2013 |archive-date=5 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305144419/http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fc/fiba/fibahist/p/opennodeids/987/selnodeid/987/fibahist.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> that separated the results of SFR Yugoslavia/FR Yugoslavia and Serbia and Montenegro respectively into "Yugoslavia" or "Serbia and Montenegro". The ranking of teams between the latter two medal tables are different, with the FIBA.com ranking by number of total medals, while the FIBA World Cup website's ranking is by number of gold medals. The number of medals won by the United States differs between the latter two medal tables, despite encompassing the same period. The latter two medal tables also do not include the results of the 2010 and 2014 championships.

Finally, a FIBA.com PDF linked from the FIBA.com history section that documents the championships from 1950 to 2002 also has a medal table that included tournaments from 1950 to 1998, which also separated pre-breakup Yugoslavia, called as "Yusgoslavia" {{sic}} from the post-breakup Yugoslavia, called as "Serbia and Montenegro", and ranked the teams by the number of total medals.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fiba.com/downloads/v3_abouFiba/mp/FIBA_world_championships_history.pdf |title=WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP MEDAL TABLE 1950-1998 |work=FIBA.com |access-date=16 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927204202/http://www.fiba.com/downloads/v3_abouFiba/mp/FIBA_world_championships_history.pdf |archive-date=27 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The FIBA archive also lists the achievements of each national team, separating it per IOC codes. The national team representing Serbia's first international tournament is listed as 2007,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp//tid/96799/_//teams.html |title=FIBA.com archive |work=FIBA.com |access-date=14 September 2014 |archive-date=30 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140830001550/http://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp/tid/96799/_/teams.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Serbia and Montenegro's tournament participation lasted from 2003 to 2006,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp//tid/92330/_//teams.html |title=FIBA.com archive |work=FIBA.com |access-date=14 September 2014 |archive-date=30 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140830104940/http://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp/tid/92330/_/teams.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> and Yugoslavia's participation was from 1947 to 2002.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp//tid/390/_//teams.html |title=FIBA.com archive |work=FIBA.com |access-date=14 September 2014 |archive-date=16 September 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140916043510/http://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp/tid/390/_/teams.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Chinese Taipei was listed not to have participated in the World Cup, indeed its first participation in any FIBA tournament started in 1986;<ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp//tid/370/_//teams.html|title=FIBA.com archive|work=FIBA.com|access-date=14 September 2014|archive-date=3 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140903021500/http://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp/tid/370/_/teams.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> a team called "Taiwan" participated from 1960 to 1973,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp//tid/5179/_//teams.html |title=FIBA.com archive |work=FIBA.com |access-date=14 September 2014 |archive-date=26 November 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151126180225/http://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp//tid/5179/_//teams.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> and a "Formosa" team joined from 1954 to 1959.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp//tid/2800/_//teams.html |title=FIBA.com archive |work=FIBA.com |access-date=14 September 2014 |archive-date=26 November 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151126180816/http://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/p/rpp//tid/2800/_//teams.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Below is the FIBA table as seen from the FIBA official website, updated with results since 1998. The records of SFR Yugoslavia and FR Yugoslavia (counted together as "Yugoslavia") are separated from records of Serbia, and Serbia and Montenegro. In the case of the Soviet Union, their records also didn't carry over to Russia.<ref name="FIBA official website"/>

==Other records and statistics==
{{main|FIBA Basketball World Cup records}}

Thirteen players&nbsp;– [[Ubiratan Pereira Maciel|Ubiratan "Bira" Pereira Maciel]], [[Marcel de Souza (basketball)|Marcel de Souza]], [[Marcelinho Machado]], [[Anderson Varejão]], [[Leandro Barbosa]], [[Alex Garcia (basketball)|Alex Garcia]] and [[Marcelo Huertas]] of [[Brazil men's national basketball team|Brazil]], [[Phil Smyth]] of [[Australia men's national basketball team|Australia]], [[Daniel Santiago]] and [[Jerome Mincy]] of [[Puerto Rico men's national basketball team|Puerto Rico]], [[Eduardo Mingas]] of [[Angola men's national basketball team|Angola]], [[Luis Scola]] of [[Argentina men's national basketball team|Argentina]] and [[Rudy Fernández (basketball)|Rudy Fernández]] of [[Spain men's national basketball team|Spain]]&nbsp;– [[FIBA Basketball World Cup records#Players with the most tournaments and games played|have appeared in five tournaments]].<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.fiba.com/downloads/v3_abouFiba/mp/FIBA_world_championships_records.pdf |title=FIBA World Championships Records|date=1 January 2007 |publisher=FIBA.com |access-date=7 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204123217/http://www.fiba.com/downloads/v3_abouFiba/mp/FIBA_world_championships_records.pdf |archive-date=4 December 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.fiba.basketball/basketballworldcup/2019/news/luis-scola-climbs-to-second-place-in-the-all-time-scoring-list |title=All time top scorers |access-date=4 September 2019 |archive-date=4 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190904212125/http://www.fiba.basketball/basketballworldcup/2019/news/luis-scola-climbs-to-second-place-in-the-all-time-scoring-list |url-status=live }}</ref>

Brazilian legend [[Oscar Schmidt]] is the runaway [[FIBA Basketball World Cup records#All-time top cumulative points scorers|all-time leading scorer]], scoring 906 career points in four tournaments between [[1978 FIBA World Championship|1978]] and [[1990 FIBA World Championship|1990]]. [[Nikos Galis]] of [[Greece men's national basketball team|Greece]] is the all-time leading scorer for a single tournament, averaging 33.7 points per game for the Greeks at the [[1986 FIBA World Championship]].

Serbian coach and former player [[Željko Obradović]] is the only person who won the title both as a coach and a player. He was a member of the [[Yugoslavia men's national basketball team|Yugoslavia team]] that won the [[1990 FIBA World Championship]] and coached the Yugoslavia team that won the [[1998 FIBA World Championship]].

==Awards==
{{main|FIBA Basketball World Cup Most Valuable Player}}
{{main|FIBA Basketball World Cup Top Scorer}}

FIBA names a [[FIBA World Cup MVP|Most Valuable Player for each tournament]]. Since the tournament opened to NBA players at the [[1994 FIBA World Championship|1994 tournament]] for the first time, [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] players have won seven of the eight MVP trophies awarded&nbsp;– [[Shaquille O'Neal]] for the [[United States national basketball team|United States]] in 1994, Germany's [[Dirk Nowitzki]] at the [[2002 FIBA World Championship|2002 tournament]], Spain's [[Pau Gasol]] at the [[2006 FIBA World Championship|2006 tournament]], [[Kevin Durant]] for the United States at the [[2010 FIBA World Championship|2010 tournament]], [[Kyrie Irving]] for the United States at the [[2014 FIBA World Championship|2014 tournament]], Spain's [[Ricky Rubio]] at the [[2019 FIBA Basketball World Cup|2019 tournament]] and Germany's [[Dennis Schröder]] at the [[2023 FIBA Basketball World Cup|2023 tournament]]. The only exception was [[Dejan Bodiroga]] of [[Serbia and Montenegro national basketball team|FR Yugoslavia]], who was the MVP of the [[1998 FIBA World Championship|1998 tournament]], when the NBA players were not able to participate due to the [[1998–99 NBA lockout]].

==Tournament growth and popularity==
===2006 Tournament===
At the 2006 championship, the accumulated TV audience figure was 800 million viewers.<ref>{{cite web |title=PR N° 17 – Turkey ready for Giant Get-Together |url=https://www.fiba.basketball/news/PR-N--17-Turkey-ready-for-Giant-Get-Together |website=FIBA |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref>

===2010 Tournament===
The [[2010 FIBA World Championship]] reached a global TV audience of close to 1 billion people in nearly 200 countries.<ref name="2010 numbers"/> Both numbers broke the previous records set at the [[2006 FIBA World Championship]] and at the [[EuroBasket 2009]].<ref name="2010 numbers"/> Three of the games involving [[Lithuania men's national basketball team|Lithuania]] were among the highest rated programs in that country. In China, 65 million watched the [[Chinese national basketball team|Chinese national team]]'s game against [[Greek national basketball team|Greece]], in the preliminary round.<ref name="2010 numbers">{{Cite web|url = http://turkey2010.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/news/p/nid/44596/article.html|title = FIBA announces most successful championship ever|date = 12 September 2010|access-date = 1 June 2014|website = Official 2010 FIBA World Championship website|publisher = [[FIBA]]|archive-date = 2 June 2014|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140602200309/http://turkey2010.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/10/fwcm/news/p/nid/44596/article.html|url-status = dead}}</ref> This was an improvement from the 2006 FIBA World Championship, which was held in Japan, and was shown in 150 countries. This meant that games aired in the morning in Europe and at night in the Americas; despite this, audiences broke records, with [[Italian national basketball team|Italy]]'s game against [[Slovenian national basketball team|Slovenia]] achieving a 20% viewing share in Italy, [[Serbian national basketball team|Serbia]]'s game against [[Nigerian national basketball team|Nigeria]] netting a 33% share in Serbia, and a 600,000-audience in the [[United States]] for the [[United States men's national basketball team|US national team]]'s game against [[Puerto Rican national basketball team|Puerto Rico]] at 1&nbsp;am.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/06_wcm/news/lateNews/p/newsid/15923/FE_news_lateNews_arti.html|title = PR no.21: Strong TV ratings for FIBA World Championship|date = 24 August 2006|access-date = 1 June 2014|website = Official 2006 FIBA World Championship website|publisher = FIBA|archive-date = 5 June 2014|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140605052258/http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/06_wcm/news/lateNews/p/newsid/15923/FE_news_lateNews_arti.html|url-status = dead}}</ref>

Before the 2010 FIBA World Championship started in Turkey, FIBA had already sold 350,000 tickets, for a revenue of between [[United States dollar|US$]]8 to 10 million. The number of tickets sold was 10% higher than 2006, although the revenue was less than 2006's US$18&nbsp;million, which was widely attributed to the strong [[Japanese yen]]. Meanwhile, FIBA got two-thirds of marketing rights revenue, of which one-third, or about US$8&nbsp;million, went to the local organizers. FIBA had also successfully negotiated TV rights deals, which all went to FIBA, worth US$25&nbsp;million, including a TV rights deal with [[ESPN]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.sportsbusinessdaily.com/Journal/Issues/2010/08/20100823/This-Weeks-News/FIBA-Event-Expects-Revenue-Jump.aspx |title=FIBA event expects revenue jump |first=John |last=Lombardo |work=Sports Business Journal |date=23 August 2010 |access-date=3 June 2014 |archive-date=7 June 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140607012728/http://www.sportsbusinessdaily.com/Journal/Issues/2010/08/20100823/This-Weeks-News/FIBA-Event-Expects-Revenue-Jump.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2006, the Japanese organizers were targeting to sell 180,000 tickets, mostly to a Japanese audience; as for the overseas audience, the Japanese organizers didn't "expect them in great numbers". This was seen as a big improvement from the [[2002 FIBA World Championship|2002 tournament]], which was a financial loss for [[USA Basketball]] and [[Indianapolis]], in which all games were held in one city. This led to the Japanese organizers to hold games throughout the country, instead of just in a single city.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2004/12/17/more-sports/fiba-likes-japans-plan-for-2006-world-championships/#.U40jPHbm4-4 |title=FIBA likes Japan's plan for 2006 world championships |first=Jack |last=Gallagher |work=[[Japan Times]] |date=17 December 2004 |access-date=3 June 2014 |archive-date=7 June 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140607001008/http://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2004/12/17/more-sports/fiba-likes-japans-plan-for-2006-world-championships/#.U40jPHbm4-4 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===2014 Tournament===
At the re-branded [[2014 FIBA Basketball World Cup]], in [[Spain]], [[FIBA]] reported impressive ratings from nations which were participating in the tournament during the first week of the group phase. Most games involving European teams had a [[market share]] of at least 20%, including a 40% market share in [[Finland]], for the [[Finnish national basketball team|Finnish national team]]'s game against the [[Dominican Republic national basketball team|Dominican Republic]].<ref>{{cite news|title=PR N°51 – Spain 2014 Group Phase games register strong audience figures on Spanish broadcaster Cuatro and all around the world|url=https://www.fiba.basketball/basketballworldcup/2014/news/PR-N-51-Spain-2014-Group-Phase-games-register-stron|access-date=28 January 2017|publisher=FIBA.com|date=5 September 2014|archive-date=12 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181112141530/http://www.fiba.basketball/basketballworldcup/2014/news/PR-N-51-Spain-2014-Group-Phase-games-register-stron|url-status=live}}</ref> The TV ratings in the United States beat out the [[2014 US Open (tennis)|2014 US Tennis Open]], but some US sports media still described viewers in the US as not caring about the FIBA Basketball World Cup.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Ziller|first1=Tom|title=Americans don't watch the FIBA World Cup|url=https://www.sbnation.com/nba/2014/9/5/6109763/fiba-world-cup-american-tv-ratings-horrible|access-date=28 January 2017|work=SBNation.com|publisher=[[SB Nation]]|date=5 September 2014|archive-date=2 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202063734/http://www.sbnation.com/nba/2014/9/5/6109763/fiba-world-cup-american-tv-ratings-horrible|url-status=live}}</ref> In the Philippines, the entire tournament had an average reach of 67.8%.<ref>{{cite news|title=PBA, FIBA World Cup are Filipinos' most watched sports events of 2014; UFC, FIFA World Cup also had many viewers – study {{!}} InterAksyon.com {{!}} Sports5|url=http://www.interaksyon.com/interaktv/pba-fiba-world-cup-are-filipinos-most-watched-sports-events-of-2014-ufc-fifa-world-cup-also-had-many-viewers-study|access-date=28 January 2017|work=InterAksyon.com|date=4 December 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202044857/http://www.interaksyon.com/interaktv/pba-fiba-world-cup-are-filipinos-most-watched-sports-events-of-2014-ufc-fifa-world-cup-also-had-many-viewers-study|archive-date=2 February 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===2019 Tournament===
According to FIBA, the TV audience for the 2019 tournament reached 3 billion, with a further 1.5 billion views on social media.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fiba World Cup sets record 3bn TV viewership |url=https://www.sportspromedia.com/news/fiba-world-cup-tv-viewing-figures-three-billion/?zephr_sso_ott=0rS39a |website=Sports Pro Media |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="2019 figures">{{cite web |title=Basketball world cup smashes records with 3 billion reach |url=https://www.digitaltveurope.com/2019/10/04/basketball-world-cup-smashes-records-with-3-billion-reach/ |website=Digital TV Europe |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref> A total of 160 million people around the world watched Spain defeat Argentina in the final.<ref name="2019 figures"/> In Spain over 10 million tuned into the final while 6.2 million watched the full game, making it the country’s most successful basketball game ever.<ref name="2019 numbers">{{cite web |title=Biggest-ever FIBA World Cup reaches record-breaking three billion people |url=https://www.fiba.basketball/news/biggest-ever-fiba-world-cup-reaches-record-breaking-three-billion-people |website=FIBA |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref> The tournament’s average TV audience increased by more than 80% from 2014.<ref name="2019 figures"/> On-site attendance also increased, with the total attendance reaching 794,951.<ref name="2019 numbers"/>

===2023 Tournament===
The total attendance for the 2023 tournament was 700,665, including the record-breaking FIBA Basketball World Cup crowd of 38,115 at the [[Philippine Arena]] for the game between the co-hosts and the Dominican Republic.<ref name="2023 final">{{cite web |title=Record-breaking engagement at the most followed FIBA Basketball World Cup ever |url=https://www.fiba.basketball/basketballworldcup/2023/news/record-breaking-engagement-at-the-most-followed-fiba-basketball-world-cup-ever#:~:text=Fans%20also%20came%20in%20big,hosts%20and%20the%20Dominican%20Republic. |website=FIBA |access-date=31 March 2024}}</ref> In Germany 5.9 million viewers (4.6 million on ZDF, plus 1.3 million on MagentaSport) watched the final between Germany and Serbia.<ref name="2023 final"/>
